the mechanisms by which the Ca2+‐activated K+ channels in the outer segments of retinal cones are controlled.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of Ca2 on the cone membrane are not consistent with the hypothesis that the Ca2‐dependent conductance is the basis of the photoresponse.
the action of Ca2+ is to reduce the number of channels open in darkness and that the effect of EGTA is to increase the number of channels which are normally open by Ca2+ ions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cone membrane has at least two different types of Ca2+‐dependent conductances, one which is closed in the dark and opens in response to light, the other which is closed by light and opens when Ca2+ is present.
the cone membrane contains two types of channels: one type is opened by Ca2+ and is closed by light and the other is closed by Ca2+.
the effects of EGTA and Ca2+ on cones are not consistent with a simple hypothesis in which Ca2+ is a second messenger of photoresponse.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca2+ plays an important role in regulating the activity of retinotectal neurons, and this role is not limited to a single cell type or region of the retina.
the cone photoresponse is a complex process that is affected by a number of variables.
the Ca2+ concentration in the extracellular medium can be a powerful regulator of the cone membrane conductance and of the kinetics and amplitude of the responses to light.
